summary: The bronze altar, basin made from women's mirrors, and linen-enclosed court are completed. A materials account then names the responsible workers and oversight, reports totals of gold, silver, and bronze, and connects the counted men's half-shekel payments to the silver bases and fittings.
whyItMatters: The sanctuary's outer working space is joined to a record of how communal materials were used. The basin preserves a specific contribution from women, while the metal accounting makes the scale and allocation of resources part of the story.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: The sanctuary construction in the Israelite camp, including the outer court and the accounting of supplied metals.
context.literaryForm: Construction narrative followed by a named administrative and materials inventory.

before.text: The ark, table, lamp stand, incense altar, oil, and incense have been made. This WEB chapter continues with the outer altar and court before totaling materials.

here.text: Bronze dominates the outer equipment, while the final account links counted contributions to particular fittings and names those responsible for the work.

after.text: The next chapter makes the priestly garments and then brings the completed work to Moses for inspection and blessing.

outline.heading: The bronze altar and its implements
outline.note: A hollow wooden altar is overlaid with bronze and fitted for sacrifice and carrying.

outline.heading: The basin from women’s mirrors
outline.note: A specific donated material is used for the bronze washing vessel and base.

outline.heading: The court and embroidered gateway
outline.note: Linen hangings, pillars, metal fittings, and pins enclose the space.

outline.heading: Named oversight and makers
outline.note: Moses’ command, Ithamar’s role, and Bezalel and Oholiab’s work frame the account.

outline.heading: Gold and silver totals and uses
outline.note: The counted half-shekels supply the silver bases and other fittings.

outline.heading: Bronze totals and uses
outline.note: The offering supplies bases, altar equipment, and pins.

keyVerses.text: He made the basin of bronze, and its base of bronze, out of the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
keyVerses.why: The basin’s material is traced to the mirrors of women serving at the tent entrance.

keyVerses.text: These are the amounts of materials used for the tabernacle, even the Tabernacle of the Testimony, as they were counted, according to the commandment of Moses, for the service of the Levites, by the hand of Ithamar, the son of Aaron the priest.
keyVerses.why: The materials account names a command and an overseeing priestly figure.

keyVerses.text: a beka a head, that is, half a shekel, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, for everyone who passed over to those who were counted, from twenty years old and upward, for six hundred three thousand five hundred fifty men.
keyVerses.why: The silver total is tied to a stated number of counted men and a half-shekel per head.

questions.question: What features of the altar show that it is meant for use and movement?
questions.answer: The account names pots, shovels, basins, forks, and fire pans as well as a grating and carrying poles. Its hollow plank construction and fitted rings make it equipment for repeated sacrificial work in a portable sanctuary.

questions.question: What can be said about the women whose mirrors become the basin?
questions.answer: They are described as ministering at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and their bronze mirrors supply the vessel and its base. The chapter does not specify their duties or motives, so it identifies their service and material contribution without a fuller institutional description.

questions.question: How is the court’s entrance distinguished from its sides?
questions.answer: The surrounding hangings are fine linen, while the gate screen uses colored embroidery. Its twenty-cubit width occupies the center of the east side between two fifteen-cubit stretches, making a defined entrance within the fifty-cubit side.

questions.question: Who is named in connection with the material account?
questions.answer: The accounting follows Moses' command and is associated with Levite service under Ithamar, Aaron's son. Bezalel and Oholiab are then identified as the makers, distinguishing administrative responsibility from their craft roles.

questions.question: What is a “beka” in the silver account?
questions.answer: The chapter itself defines it as half a shekel according to the sanctuary standard. One is assigned per counted man aged twenty and upward, linking the head count directly to the amount collected.

questions.question: How does the silver account connect amounts with the building?
questions.answer: One hundred talents are assigned to one hundred sanctuary and veil sockets, one talent per base. The remaining 1,775 shekels are used for hooks, overlaid capitals, and bands, so the total is broken into stated construction uses.

questions.question: Does the stated census count include every person in the camp?
questions.answer: The figure is specifically 603,550 counted men aged twenty and upward. It is not presented as a total including women and children, and the materials account supplies no separate full-population count.

questions.question: What work receives the bronze total?
questions.answer: The list assigns bronze to entrance and court sockets, the altar and grating, altar vessels, and the tent and court pins. The account closes by connecting the supplied metal to the outer structure's supports and working equipment.

glossary.def: Half a shekel, explicitly defined here as the contribution per counted man.
A large weight unit used alongside shekels in the account of metals.
The tops of the pillars, which receive the specified metal covering.
